Map your system's data flows, showing how data moves through the different components.
Analyze how each of the six STRIDE threat categories could affect each component or data flow.

Threat
Concrete attack scenario
Patient (external entity)
S
Attacker steals credentials and impersonates the patient submitting forged "healthy" images to suppress alerts for a patient with a real infection.
T
Patient deliberately submits a manipulated or outdated image to bypass monitoring (intentional misuse).

S

T

Processes
Flutter App
S
Repackaged/trojanised APK impersonates the legitimate app, harvesting credentials before forwarding them.
T
On a rooted phone, a malicious app intercepts and modifies the image bytes before they are sent to the backend.
R
No client side submission receipt patient can claim they submitted an assessment when they did not (or vice versa).
I
App caches assessment results and images unencrypted on the device, another app or person with physical access can read them.
D
Backend unreachable → app freezes with no offline fallback, preventing the patient from completing their daily check in.
E
Jailbroken device bypasses app sandboxing; attacker reads another user's stored token from app storage and escalates session.
Clinician Dashboard
S
Session token stolen and attacker assumes the clinician's identity in the browser.
T
Stored Cross-Site Scripting in a patient name field renders a malicious script that changes displayed CLISA scores for all viewing clinicians.
R
No audit trail of which clinician reviewed or dismissed a flagged case no accountability if a critical case is ignored.
I
Dashboard fetches all patient records without role based filtering a trainee with limited access sees all patients in the system.
D
DDoS on the web server makes the dashboard unavailable during a clinical shift when urgent cases need review.
E
Insecure direct object reference: clinician changes patient ID in URL and accesses another clinician's patient list.
Backend API Server
S
Forged JWT (weak signing key) lets an attacker impersonate any user including admins.
T
NoSQL injection via an unvalidated request field overwrites a stored assessment score in the database.
R
No structured request logging impossible to reconstruct which client triggered which write after an incident.
I
API response includes full patient objects when only a summary is needed over fetching exposes health information unnecessarily.
D
No rate limiting attacker floods the upload endpoint, exhausting server memory and blocking legitimate submissions.
E
Broken access control: a patient-role JWT can reach an admin endpoint that lists all users in the system.
Auth Server
S
Attacker stands up a rogue auth server on the internal network; API Server is misconfigured to trust it and accepts forged tokens.
T
Weak JWT signing key allows offline brute force attacker crafts tokens with elevated roles.
R
Failed login attempts not logged no detection of credential stuffing attacks against patient accounts.
I
JWT payload contains sensitive fields (diagnosis, clinician ID) in plaintext — readable by anyone who intercepts the token.
D
Brute force login flood locks out all patient accounts simultaneously, preventing access during an emergency check in.
E
Role field in the token is not server validated client modifies the decoded token role from "patient" to "clinician" before re encoding.
AI Inference Server
S
Inference server exposed on internal network without auth any service (or attacker with internal access) can submit images and obtain CLISA scores without going through the API Server.
T
Adversarial image attack: imperceptible pixel perturbation flips a CLISA score from 3 (concerning) to 0 (normal), suppressing a critical alert.
R
No logging of input images and output scores impossible to audit why a particular assessment was classified low risk after a patient deteriorates.
I
Model inversion attack: repeated queries reconstruct training images containing identifiable patient data (PHI exposure).
D
Oversized or malformed image causes the inference process to hang, blocking all subsequent assessment requests.
E
Prompt injection embedded in image metadata hijacks the model's output format, allowing arbitrary JSON to be returned to the backend.
Database
T
Injection attack overwrites a stored CLISA score from 3 to 0 clinician sees a normal result for a critically infected patient.
R
No row level change log after a tampered record is discovered, there is no way to tell which account made the change or when.
I
Database not encrypted at rest — a stolen backup disk exposes all patient assessments and personal health information.
D
Ransomware encrypts the database; all assessment history becomes inaccessible, preventing longitudinal monitoring.
File Storage
T
Attacker with write access replaces a stored image with a healthy looking one clinician reviews the wrong image and misses an infection.
R
No access log on the storage bucket — no record of who downloaded which patient image or when.
I
Misconfigured storage permissions make the image bucket publicly accessible — anyone with the URL can view patient photos.
D
Storage volume fills up; new image uploads fail silently patients believe their assessment was submitted but no image reaches the clinician.
Assess the potential impact of each threat on patient safety and healthcare delivery.
3. Assess the potential impact of each threat on patient safety and healthcare delivery.
Impact assessment — patient safety & healthcare delivery
Threats are grouped by severity. Each card shows the patient safety consequence and the healthcare delivery consequence separately.
Critical: Direct risk to patient life or irreversible harm
Adversarial image flips CLISA score 3 → 0 (Tampering · AI Inference Server):
Patient safety:

A patient with a severely infected catheter site receives a "normal" assessment result. No alert is raised, no clinician reviews the case. The infection progresses untreated to CLABSI — a bloodstream infection with ~25% mortality in oncology patients.
Healthcare delivery:

The monitoring system actively produces false reassurance. Clinicians trust the AI output and do not follow up. The entire purpose of SITE is inverted — it becomes a tool that conceals infections rather than detecting them.
CLISA score overwritten in database (Tampering · Database):
Patient safety:

A stored score of 3 (escalate) is changed to 0 (normal). The clinician dashboard shows no flagged cases. Critical cases go unreviewed and untreated — patient deterioration goes undetected until an emergency admission.
Healthcare delivery:

Corrupted records destroy the integrity of longitudinal monitoring. Trend analysis (is this patient getting worse over time?) becomes meaningless. Clinical decisions based on historical data are built on falsified evidence.
Rogue auth server issues arbitrary tokens (Spoofing · Auth Server):
Patient safety:
Attacker gains clinician-level access and systematically dismisses all escalated cases. Multiple high-risk patients lose their only remote monitoring safety net simultaneously.
Healthcare delivery:

Full compromise of the authentication layer invalidates every active session. The entire system must be taken offline to rotate credentials, causing a complete monitoring blackout across all patients.
High: Significant patient safety risk or major PHI breach
Backend API unavailable (DDoS / no rate limiting) (Denial of Service · Backend API Server):
Patient safety:
Patients cannot submit their daily check-in. A patient with a rapidly advancing infection misses the window where early intervention would have been effective.
Healthcare delivery:
Clinicians receive no new assessments during the outage. If this coincides with a high-risk period (post-chemotherapy), the gap in monitoring creates unacceptable clinical risk.
Patient credentials stolen — false submissions (Spoofing · Patient):
Patient safety:
Attacker submits healthy-looking images on behalf of the patient. The real patient's deteriorating site is never assessed — their condition worsens while the system reports all clear.
Healthcare delivery:
Clinician's workload and trust in the system is unaffected — making the attack invisible. The absence of alerts is interpreted as clinical stability, not as a security incident.
Unencrypted database exposed / ransomware (Information Disclosure + Denial of Service · Database):
Patient safety:
Complete assessment history for all patients is lost or exposed. Clinicians lose the longitudinal view needed to detect gradual deterioration trends across multiple check-ins.
Healthcare delivery:
GDPR / medical data breach notification required. Potential MDR regulatory action. Patient trust in digital health monitoring collapses — patients may refuse future remote monitoring programmes.
Patient images publicly accessible (open storage bucket) (Information Disclosure · File Storage):
Patient safety:

Intimate wound-site photographs are exposed publicly. Psychological harm to patients who learn their images were visible. Chilling effect — patients stop submitting photos, removing the core monitoring input.
Healthcare delivery:
Mandatory GDPR data breach reporting. If the breach involves images of minors or identifiable patients, criminal liability may apply. The programme would likely be suspended pending investigation.
Patient role escalated to clinician via broken access control (Elevation of Privilege · Backend API / Auth Server):
Patient safety:
Attacker can view, modify, or dismiss cases for all patients in the system — not just their own. A single compromised patient account becomes a threat to the entire patient population.
Healthcare delivery:
Clinicians can no longer trust the integrity of the dashboard — any case dismissal or score could have been made by an unauthorised actor. The system must be audited before clinical use can resume.

Medium-severity threats (Repudiation: missing clinician audit log; Tampering: XSS in clinician dashboard; Denial of Service: auth server outage; Information Disclosure: unencrypted PHI cached on device) cause operational disruption or indirect patient risk but do not directly harm patients. Low-severity threats (Repudiation: missing submission receipt; Denial of Service: silent image drop on storage throttle) are contained and have operational workarounds with no direct patient impact.
Propose mitigation measures to reduce the identified risks.
4. Propose mitigation measures to reduce the identified risks.
S — Spoofing
Multi-factor authentication for clinicians:
Clinicians authenticate with a second factor (TOTP or hardware key); a stolen password alone cannot grant access to patient data.
Rate limiting and account lockout on the Auth Server:
After a configurable number of failed attempts the account is locked and an alert is sent, blocking credential-stuffing attacks.
Strong JWT validation on the Backend API Server:
Every inbound JWT is verified against the Auth Server’s public key and rejected if the issuer, audience, or expiry does not match.
Mutual TLS between internal services:
Both the API Server and Auth Server present mutual TLS certificates, so a rogue internal service cannot impersonate either.
Certificate pinning in the Flutter app:
The app pins the backend’s TLS certificate and refuses connections that do not match, blocking MITM attacks on untrusted networks.
T — Tampering
TLS 1.2+ enforced on all network channels, including internal:
All data in transit is encrypted with TLS 1.2+ on every channel, including internal service-to-service traffic; plain HTTP is rejected.
Image integrity hashing:
A SHA-256 hash is computed on upload and re-verified on retrieval; any mismatch causes the request to be rejected.
Parameterised queries / ORM for all database operations:
All database operations use parameterised queries or a typed ORM, eliminating injection as a tampering path.
Output encoding and Content Security Policy on the Clinician Dashboard:
User-supplied strings are HTML-encoded before rendering and a strict Content Security Policy blocks inline script execution.
Adversarial robustness testing of the AI model:
The model is tested against known perturbation techniques and low-confidence outputs trigger manual clinician review instead of an automatic score.
R — Repudiation
Structured, append-only audit log:
Every state-changing action is written to a tamper-evident, append-only log with timestamp, user ID, and IP address.
Server-side submission receipts:
The Backend API Server returns a signed receipt to the Flutter app on every successful assessment submission.
Clinician action logging:
Case views, dismissals, and assignments are logged per clinician to support medico-legal accountability.
I — Information Disclosure
Encryption at rest for database and file storage:
Both the database and file storage are encrypted with AES-256 at rest; a stolen backup or disk exposes no readable patient data.
Principle of least privilege on API responses:
Endpoints return only the fields the client needs for that operation, not full patient objects.
JWT payload minimisation:
The token contains only user ID and role — no diagnosis, clinical history, or other PHI.
Encrypted local storage on the Flutter app:
Cached data is stored using platform encrypted storage (Android Keystore / iOS Secure Enclave) and purged on logout.
Private storage bucket with pre-signed URLs:
The bucket is not publicly accessible; short-lived pre-signed URLs scoped to a single file are issued per access request.
No secrets in source code:
Credentials and keys are injected at runtime via environment variables or a secrets manager, never hardcoded in source.
D — Denial of Service
Rate limiting on all public endpoints:
Per-IP and per-user request limits are enforced; upload endpoints have stricter limits than read endpoints.
Maximum file size enforcement:
Uploads above the defined size limit are rejected before being read into memory, preventing resource exhaustion.
Timeout and circuit breaker on the AI Inference Server:
Hard timeouts on inference calls prevent thread starvation; timed-out requests return a manual-review flag rather than blocking other users.
Auth Server redundancy:
Multiple instances run behind a load balancer; cached public keys allow local token verification during brief outages.
Offline submission queue in the Flutter app:
Failed submissions are stored in encrypted local storage and retried automatically when the connection is restored.
E — Elevation of Privilege
Server-side role enforcement on every endpoint:
Role checks run on the Backend API Server for every request; client-side role claims are never trusted without server-side validation.
Resource ownership validation (prevent IDOR):
The server confirms the requesting user is authorized for the specific patient record before returning any data, preventing IDOR.
Short-lived tokens with mandatory refresh:
JWTs expire after a short window; refresh token rotation invalidates the previous token on each use, limiting theft impact.
Separate service accounts with minimal permissions:
Internal services connect to the database with minimal-permission accounts scoped only to the tables they need.
